title: Murmur: Efficient Long-Context ASR Inference with Hierarchical Chunking
story_key: story|title:murmur efficient long context asr inference with hierarchical chunking
content_excerpt: TL;DR: Murmur speeds up long-context ASR models on audio up to 1 hour by 2.5× on average (up to 2.9×), end to end including diarization. It also lowers speaker-attributed error (tcpWER) compared with WhisperX by 7-17 points on English meetings and 10-51 points on Mandarin. Single pass, Murmur, and WhisperX transcribing the same 32-minute AMI meeting on one H100, replayed at 8×. Recent long-context ASR models, such as Microsoft VibeVoice-ASR and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize, process an hour or more of audio in a single pass. They generate text, timestamps and speaker labels at the same time. An hour of audio is tens of thousands of audio tokens (about 27,000 for VibeVoice-ASR), so a single pass is slow: on one H100, VibeVoice-ASR takes about 2.5 minutes to transcribe a 44-minute meeting. These models can also fall into a repetition loop, which makes the whole request fail. The other common approach is to split the recording into short chunks, such as the 30 s chunks WhisperX uses for Whisper. Timestamps and speaker labels then have to be stitched together across hundreds of chunk boundaries, which lowers accuracy, especially in speaker attribution. This design was built for short-context models, while long-context models can take in minutes of audio at once. Neither option fits long-context models well. We revisit how long audio should be chunked and served for these models, and design Murmur, an inference system that closes the gap between the two approaches. We first study how chunk size affects long-context ASR. Across 4 datasets and 2 languages (English and Mandarin), error drops quickly as chunks grow from 30 s and levels off within a few minutes (Figure 1). At 330 s, chunked decoding already improves on or matches single pass on word error rate (WER) and time-constrained word error rate (tcpWER) in most cases, so the model does not need the whole recording in one pass. Figure 1. Error vs. chunk size (30-390 s) for MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize and VibeVoice-ASR on four meeting datasets. Dashed lines are single pass. Error drops quickly from 30 s and levels off by about 150-330 s, mostly on the speaker metrics (cpWER, tcpWER). Figure 2. (a) WhisperX decodes 30 s segments independently and adds timestamps and speakers afterwards. (b) Long-context models decode the whole recording in one pass. title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

title: CrossEnv: Synthesizing Verifiable Cross-Environment Tasks for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Executable synthetic environments provide scalable training tasks and verifiable feedback for long-horizon agents. Existing environment synthesis methods primarily generate tasks within individual environments. However, these tasks do not adequately capture real-world interactions across services, where actions in one service depend on information obtained from another. Synthesizing such tasks is challenging because data generated across environments must remain consistent to support executable and verifiable interactions. To address this challenge, we introduce CrossEnv, a framework that uses an entity-tool graph to identify connections between environments and aligns task-specific data to synthesize executable, verifiable cross-environment tasks. We further propose CrossEnv-Curriculum, which progresses from single-environment tool use to coordination across more environments and business domains, before introducing user interaction. Across four external benchmarks, combining cross-environment training data with this curriculum achieves competitive performance with fewer training examples. Further analyses support the benefits of cross-environment data and curriculum training, and provide evidence of transfer to new environment combinations, external tasks less similar to the training data, and longer workflows.

title: AI-assisted code at scale: provenance, quality, centrality and review time
story_key: story|title:ai assisted code at scale provenance quality centrality and review time
content_excerpt: A Preliminary Analysis of the Impact of AI Assisted/Generated Code on Quality, Centrality and Review Time at Scale — Audris Mockus, Peter C. Rigby, Don Stewart, Chandra Maddila, and Nachiappan Nagappan. ESEM 2026, Software Engineering in Practice track, Munich, 8–9 Oct 2026. LIPIcs vol. 394, pp. 93:1–93:23. This is the first published peer-reviewed piece on the code provenance system I’ve been working on for the last two years. The core idea: track every character’s provenance. Identify AI authorship through the characters changed in files, and track the change through source control — using accurate filesystem and source-control-based analysis, not heuristics. What we found, across 10,000+ developers and 400,000 diffs at Meta: AI-assisted code lands more in less central code, in larger changes, in test files, and from higher-tenure authors. Review time goes down and severe-incident rates are lower for diffs with AI code — though both are confounded by the fact that AI code shows up in less central contexts to begin with.

title: Why we rebuilt LangSmith around the agent
summary: We reorganized LangSmith around a single agent record. Build, run, improve, and govern every agent from one place, on any framework or runtime.
story_key: story|title:why we rebuilt langsmith around the agent
content_excerpt: Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform : a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business. In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next. 2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses , models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work . Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models. Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing , monitoring , and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals. AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened. We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it. LangSmith supports the entire agent development lifecycle: build, run, improve, and govern. Now, we've connected the entire process through a unique agent record. When you open an agent record, its traces, evals, Agent Server, and Engine issues are accessible with one click, so you don’t need to navigate multiple surfaces to find them. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple. LangSmith is composable, so you can choose the parts you need. If you already run your agent on another platform, you can connect it to LangSmith to improve and govern it without changing any other workflows. title: When Passing Checks Do Not Establish Completion: Evidence Interpretation in Coding Agents
summary: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope and discharge checking obligations. We study these responsibilities through qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers and executable workflows. A prospective thirteen-task factorial study finds that correct reported facts need not yield the requested finite verdict. Conversely, all 122 delivered labels in a held-out receipt-supply study are correct, while sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven others exceed authorized scope. Production repair supplies successful controls and finite-supported preservation failures. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from the claimed operation. Lifetime and resource controls delimit what passing validation establishes. Generated-note comparisons yield local repair differences but can state false explanations; strong ordinary baselines, new tasks and Skill-transfer studies supply no consistent overall advantage. These results characterize evidence interpretation, applicability and fulfilled actions while limiting claims of general diagnostic superiority, Skill deterioration or deployed folding effects.

title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
summary: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.

title: llm 0.37.3
summary:
Release: llm 0.37.3

A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According to D. Richard Hipp:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

title: Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
story_key: model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation in vllm scaling multimodal serving with epd
content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings.
